screens.title: Least Privilege
screens.narratorSegment: Least privilege means assigning the smallest set of rights required for a user, process, or service to perform its function. The rationale is simple: every additional permission increases the potential damage if that identity is compromised. For example, a web server that only serves static files does not need root privileges. If the server process has only read access to the served files and no write access to system directories, a vulnerability exploited in the web application will be limited in its impact. A concrete exercise is to inspect the user and group ownership of a service process and reduce its capabilities, for instance by running services under dedicated service users and restricting their file access to specific directories. A common misconception is that fewer permissions will break functionality. Mitigate that by testing in a staging VM and using incremental permission tightening: remove write access first, verify service behavior, then remove read access where possible. Key takeaway: least privilege reduces blast radius and makes incidents easier to contain. Ask yourself which accounts on your system currently hold more permissions than they need.

keyIdea.title: Reduce blast radius

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Least Privilege
What least privilege means
Limit rights for users and services to only what they need to operate.
Common approach
  • Create dedicated service accounts.
  • Restrict file and directory access to service-owned paths.
  • Use sudo to grant specific elevated commands when necessary.
Misconception
Removing permissions will break services. Instead, tighten incrementally and test in staging before production.
Key Takeaway

Design accounts with the minimum rights needed and validate functionality through staged testing.

Concrete example
Run a web server as its own user and give that user only the directory that contains static files.
# Create a service user and directory
sudo useradd --system --no-create-home wwwsvc
sudo mkdir -p /srv/www/example
sudo chown wwwsvc:wwwsvc /srv/www/example
sudo chmod 750 /srv/www/example
This limits access to the web content and prevents the server process from writing to other system paths. If an exploit allows code execution under the web server account, the attacker cannot modify system configuration files that remain owned by root.
Check your understanding
List two accounts on your system and state whether their current permissions match the minimum needed privileges.

screens.title: Defense in Depth
screens.narratorSegment: Defense in depth means you do not rely on a single control to protect your systems. Instead, you layer firewalls, strong authentication, access controls, logging, and patch management so that if one line fails, another helps contain or detect the issue. For example, a misconfigured application firewall might allow traffic through, but strong authentication and proper file permissions can still prevent privilege escalation or data exfiltration. A practical application is to pair network-level filtering with host-based protections and monitoring: use a firewall to limit inbound ports, require strong passwords and multi-factor authentication for logins, restrict filesystem permissions, and enable logging so you can investigate anomalies. A common misconception is that more layers equal more complexity without benefit. In reality, thoughtful layering balances redundancy and operational maintainability; each layer should address a different class of threat. The takeaway is to design overlapping controls that together reduce the probability and impact of an incident. Consider which layer would stop an attacker who obtained valid credentials and plan compensating controls accordingly. Defense in Depth means combine network, host, auth, and monitoring controls so failures in one area are mitigated by others.. In practical terms, multiple layers of controls to catch failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Defense in Depth
Layered controls
Design each layer to address a different vulnerability class.
Network
Limit exposure with firewalls and port filtering.
Authentication
Enforce strong passwords and multi-factor controls.
Host & Files
Correct permissions, sudo policies, and service isolation.
Monitoring
Logging and intrusion detection help spot bypasses quickly.
Concrete scenario
If an attacker discovers a web app bug that lets them upload a file, network filtering can block many injection points. Proper permissions prevent that uploaded file from executing in sensitive locations. Logging will show failed access attempts, and patching closes the exploit once a fix exists.
Common Mistake

Relying on a perimeter firewall alone. Internal controls and host hardening are still necessary.

Key Takeaway

Design defenses so one failure does not lead to full compromise; each layer should be testable and auditable.

screens.title: Strong Authentication & PAM
screens.narratorSegment: Strong authentication starts with robust passwords and, when available, multi-factor authentication. On Linux, PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) provides a flexible framework to enforce policies across login methods. The pam_pwquality or pam_cracklib module is commonly used to require minimum length and character classes. Parameters such as minlen, dcredit, ucredit, lcredit, and ocredit define how many of each character type are required. For example, setting minlen to 12 and each credit parameter to -1 forces at least one digit, one uppercase, one lowercase, and one special character. A safe workflow is: first back up the existing PAM files, then change configuration in a sandbox, and verify by creating a test user to ensure weak passwords are rejected. A common pitfall is mis-editing PAM so you lock out all users; always keep a root console or rescue path available. After testing, incrementally roll the policy into production. The concrete example in the visual shows a sample pam_pwquality line and a simulated adduser attempt that fails with a weak password and succeeds with a strong one. What test will you run first to validate a new PAM policy?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Strong Authentication & PAM
PAM parameter example
# Example line in /etc/pam.d/system-auth or /etc/pam.d/password-auth
password    requisite     pam_pwquality.so try_first_pass local_users_only retry=3 minlen=14 dcredit=-1 ucredit=-1 lcredit=-1 ocredit=-1 enforce_for_root
This enforces length and requires one digit, uppercase, lowercase, and other character, and applies to root too.
Testing workflow
  1. Backup PAM files before editing.
  2. Edit in a sandbox and keep a root console for recovery.
  3. Create a test user and verify weak passwords are rejected.
Simulated terminal: adduser
$ sudo adduser testuser
Enter new UNIX password: password
BAD PASSWORD: it is too simple
Retype new UNIX password: password
Sorry, passwords must be longer and include digits and symbols
Enter new UNIX password: Str0ng!Passw0rd
Retype new UNIX password: Str0ng!Passw0rd
Adding user `testuser' ... done
The weak attempt is rejected; the strong one is accepted. This validates the pam_pwquality rules.
Caution
A bad PAM edit can lock out users. Always back up and keep a recovery shell to revert changes.

screens.title: Hands-on: Enforcing a Strong Password Policy
screens.narratorSegment: When changing authentication policies, follow a safe process: backup, modify in a sandbox, test with a test account, and revert if necessary. Start by copying critical PAM files so you can restore them. Next, edit the pam_pwquality line to set the required parameters. After saving, immediately test by adding or changing a test user's password to confirm that weak passwords are rejected and strong ones are accepted. If a problem arises, restore the backed-up files and reboot or restart the login service as necessary. The hands-on steps are short but precise: back up /etc/pam. d/system-auth and /etc/pam. d/password-auth, change the pam_pwquality parameters, run adduser or passwd for a test account, and then review logs or failure messages. A common error is skipping the backup. If you forget and lock out accounts, recovery can be time-consuming. The takeaway is that small changes to authentication are high-impact and must be reversible. After practicing, you should be able to demonstrate the change and explain why each step exists. Hands-on: Enforcing a Strong Password Policy means always back up pam files, test policies with a non-privileged test user, and keep a recovery path.. In practical terms, backup, edit, test, and revert safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Password Policy Lab
Step 1 — Backup
sudo cp /etc/pam.d/system-auth /etc/pam.d/system-auth.bak
sudo cp /etc/pam.d/password-auth /etc/pam.d/password-auth.bak
Keep backups so you can quickly restore if logins fail.
Step 2 — Edit
# Edit with visudo-like safety (use your editor)
# Change the pam_pwquality line to include: minlen=14 dcredit=-1 ucredit=-1 lcredit=-1 ocredit=-1
Step 3 — Test
sudo adduser testlab
# Try a weak password first and confirm it is rejected
# Then try a strong password and confirm success
If tests fail, restore backups immediately and troubleshoot in the sandbox.
Step 4 — Revert (optional)
sudo mv /etc/pam.d/system-auth.bak /etc/pam.d/system-auth
sudo mv /etc/pam.d/password-auth.bak /etc/pam.d/password-auth
Example check
After a successful test, document the change, why it was made, and how to roll it back. This makes future troubleshooting faster.

screens.title: Sudo: Granular Privilege vs. Full Root
screens.narratorSegment: Sudo is a mechanism to let specific users run commands with elevated privileges without handing them full root access. The safest pattern is to grant only the exact commands a person needs. For instance, giving a user permission to restart a single service is better than granting NOPASSWD for all commands. Compare two sudoers entries: one that grants all commands with NOPASSWD and one that allows only systemctl restart nginx as root. The former expands the attack surface and removes accountability, while the latter provides necessary capability for a narrow operational task. A misconception is that restricting commands is cumbersome; in practice, carefully chosen entries are clearer and auditable. Use visudo to edit /etc/sudoers and avoid syntax errors. The example in this screen shows both configurations and explains why the restricted entry adheres to least privilege. After configuring, test the sudo action as the target user and verify logs capture the command. Which commands on your systems could be limited by sudoers entries? Sudo: Granular Privilege vs. Full Root means use visudo to create least-privilege sudoers entries and test them for expected behavior and logging.. In practical terms, grant specific commands instead of blanket root access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Sudo Comparison
Dangerous: Full root
# Grants all commands without password - broad power
devops ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL
This removes check and balance and allows any command to run as root without authentication.
Preferred: Specific command
# Allow restart nginx as root without a password
devops ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx
This limits the user to a single, auditable action required for operational tasks.
Testing and logging
After updating sudoers, test by switching to the user and invoking the allowed command. Use /var/log/auth.log or the system journal to verify the command and user are recorded.
Key Takeaway

Prefer tightly scoped sudoers entries to preserve least privilege while enabling required tasks.

screens.title: File Permissions and Ownership
screens.narratorSegment: File permissions are one of the simplest and most effective defenses for sensitive data. The Unix permission model grants read, write, and execute rights for owner, group, and others. Misconfigured files like private keys or configuration files set to world-readable or world-writable create an easy path for attackers. A common secure setting for a private SSH key is 600, meaning only the owner can read and write it. A configuration file might be 640, so the owner can read and write while the group can only read. Use chown to set ownership and chmod to set modes. A misconception is that complicated ACLs are always required; often a correct owner:group and straightforward mode are sufficient. The practical example shows commands to change ownership to root:myappgroup and set mode 640. Always consider which process or user needs access and minimize permissions accordingly. The final check is to list the file with ls -l to confirm ownership and mode. Which critical file on your system needs permission correction? File Permissions and Ownership means use chown and chmod to ensure only the necessary accounts can read or modify sensitive files.. In practical terms, protect configuration and private keys with correct modes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › File Permissions
Common secure modes
  • Private SSH key: chmod 600, owner only.
  • Config files: chmod 640 with appropriate group ownership.
  • Logs: limit write access and rotate regularly.
Commands
sudo chown root:myappgroup /etc/myapp/config.yml
sudo chmod 640 /etc/myapp/config.yml
sudo chmod 600 /home/alice/.ssh/id_rsa
Before and after
# Before: world-writeable
-rw-rw-rw- 1 root root 2345 Sep 12 10:00 /etc/myapp/config.yml
# After: restricted
-rw-r----- 1 root myappgroup 2345 Sep 12 10:05 /etc/myapp/config.yml

screens.title: Sudoers and visudo: Safe edits
screens.narratorSegment: Editing sudoers must be done with care because a syntactic error can make the file unusable. The recommended tool is visudo, which checks syntax before saving. Use visudo to add narrowly scoped entries that run as root for specific commands. For example, to allow user sysadmin to restart httpd, you can add 'sysadmin ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart httpd'. If you need passwordless operation, add NOPASSWD cautiously and only for required commands. Always document why the entry exists and the expected duration. After adding entries, test by switching to the target user and invoking the command, then check /var/log/auth. log or the journal to see the sudo event recorded. A frequent misconception is that sudoers entries are permanent policy; instead, treat them as changeable operational policies that should be removed when no longer needed. Keep a central change log for sudoers modifications and consider using configuration management for repeatable, reviewed changes. Which command on your systems would benefit from a restricted sudo entry? A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Security Updates: Patch Management Basics
screens.narratorSegment: Applying security updates is one of the most practical steps to reduce risk. Vendors release patches to address newly discovered vulnerabilities, and delaying updates leaves systems exposed to known exploits. A sensible approach is to test updates in staging before applying them in production, schedule regular maintenance windows, and use your distribution's package manager to perform updates consistently. For Debian/Ubuntu use apt, and for RHEL-based systems use yum or dnf. Automating updates may be appropriate for non-critical systems, but for critical services you should validate compatibility first. Keep a changelog of applied updates and have a rollback plan — snapshots or backups can restore service quickly if a patch causes regression. A common misconception is that updates are optional if a system seems to run fine; in truth, running unpatched software is a primary cause of breaches. The takeaway is to make updates routine, tested, and auditable so you steadily close known attack paths without surprising downtime. Security Updates: Patch Management Basics means test patches in staging, schedule updates, and maintain backups so you can roll back if necessary.. In practical terms, keep software current to reduce exposure to known vulnerabilities. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Physical Security
screens.narratorSegment: Physical security is often overlooked but critical: if an attacker gains physical access to a server, many software-based protections can be circumvented. Physical controls include locked server rooms, badge access, surveillance, and limiting console access to authorized personnel. Even a desktop can be compromised by unauthorized USB devices or direct keyboard access. For servers, ensure that boot order and BIOS settings are protected and consider full disk encryption to protect data at rest if a drive is stolen. A misconception is that physical security only matters for large data centers; in fact, any machine that stores keys or credentials must be physically protected. The practical advice is to inventory where critical machines are located, restrict access, and plan for secure disposal of retired hardware. When designing physical controls, coordinate them with network and host protections so a single physical breach does not expose all systems. What small physical control could you improve right now at your workplace or home lab? Physical Security means limit physical access to servers and protect disk contents to prevent local compromise and data theft.. In practical terms, protect hardware to prevent bypass of software controls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Practical measures

fullNarratorScript:
Security is not an afterthought — it is a daily mindset built into every administrative decision. In this lesson you will learn core principles such as least privilege and defense in depth, how to enforce strong authentication and password policies with PAM, and how to use sudo and file permissions to limit damage if an account is compromised. We will also cover the role of regular updates and physical protections for servers. Each topic includes hands-on examples you can try in a safe environment, such as backing up PAM configurations, testing password policies with a test user, and using visudo to grant a limited sudo command. You will also practice checking and correcting file permissions for sensitive files like private SSH keys and configuration files. By the end you should be able to explain why minimal permissions reduce attack surface, how layered controls help resist failure, and how to apply a simple, test-first workflow when changing authentication or sudo settings. Think about one critical file on your system now and how you would restrict access to it.

These objectives define the practical skills you will build. First, you'll understand the principle of least privilege and how granting only needed permissions reduces the risk of escalation. Expect a definition, examples, and a short exercise to restrict a service account. Second, you'll apply defense in depth, mapping controls such as firewalls, authentication, and auditing into layered protections. You will learn how overlapping measures catch failures if one control is bypassed. Third, you'll implement strong password policies and practical PAM settings that enforce complexity, length, and reuse controls. The lesson includes an editable configuration example and a test workflow to verify changes in a non-production environment. Fourth, you'll review file and directory permissions and practice using chown and chmod to protect private keys and config files. Each objective is paired with a small mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you know when you're ready to move on. Keep in mind that each change should be tested and reversible, because misconfiguring authentication or permissions can lock users out or break services.

This second objectives slide focuses on applied tasks. First, you will configure PAM modules such as pam_pwquality to enforce min length and character classes. The narration and example code will show common parameters like minlen, dcredit, ucredit, lcredit, and ocredit. Second, you will practice safe sudo configuration with visudo, learning how to give a user permission to run a specific command without granting full root access. We will contrast bad sudo entries that grant NOPASSWD all access with restricted entries that limit commands and target root explicitly. Third, you will audit and fix file permissions for sensitive files using chown and chmod, and understand the security risk of world-writable or world-readable files. Finally, we will cover the importance of routine security updates and how failing to patch leaves systems vulnerable. Each objective contains a short mnemonic and a milestone you can mark complete after testing in a sandboxed environment. Remember: back up configuration files before editing so you can recover if something blocks logins.

Least privilege means assigning the smallest set of rights required for a user, process, or service to perform its function. The rationale is simple: every additional permission increases the potential damage if that identity is compromised. For example, a web server that only serves static files does not need root privileges. If the server process has only read access to the served files and no write access to system directories, a vulnerability exploited in the web application will be limited in its impact. A concrete exercise is to inspect the user and group ownership of a service process and reduce its capabilities, for instance by running services under dedicated service users and restricting their file access to specific directories. A common misconception is that fewer permissions will break functionality. Mitigate that by testing in a staging VM and using incremental permission tightening: remove write access first, verify service behavior, then remove read access where possible. Key takeaway: least privilege reduces blast radius and makes incidents easier to contain. Ask yourself which accounts on your system currently hold more permissions than they need.

Defense in depth means you do not rely on a single control to protect your systems. Instead, you layer firewalls, strong authentication, access controls, logging, and patch management so that if one line fails, another helps contain or detect the issue. For example, a misconfigured application firewall might allow traffic through, but strong authentication and proper file permissions can still prevent privilege escalation or data exfiltration. A practical application is to pair network-level filtering with host-based protections and monitoring: use a firewall to limit inbound ports, require strong passwords and multi-factor authentication for logins, restrict filesystem permissions, and enable logging so you can investigate anomalies. A common misconception is that more layers equal more complexity without benefit. In reality, thoughtful layering balances redundancy and operational maintainability; each layer should address a different class of threat. The takeaway is to design overlapping controls that together reduce the probability and impact of an incident. Consider which layer would stop an attacker who obtained valid credentials and plan compensating controls accordingly. Defense in Depth means combine network, host, auth, and monitoring controls so failures in one area are mitigated by others.. In practical terms, multiple layers of controls to catch failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Strong authentication starts with robust passwords and, when available, multi-factor authentication. On Linux, PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) provides a flexible framework to enforce policies across login methods. The pam_pwquality or pam_cracklib module is commonly used to require minimum length and character classes. Parameters such as minlen, dcredit, ucredit, lcredit, and ocredit define how many of each character type are required. For example, setting minlen to 12 and each credit parameter to -1 forces at least one digit, one uppercase, one lowercase, and one special character. A safe workflow is: first back up the existing PAM files, then change configuration in a sandbox, and verify by creating a test user to ensure weak passwords are rejected. A common pitfall is mis-editing PAM so you lock out all users; always keep a root console or rescue path available. After testing, incrementally roll the policy into production. The concrete example in the visual shows a sample pam_pwquality line and a simulated adduser attempt that fails with a weak password and succeeds with a strong one. What test will you run first to validate a new PAM policy?

When changing authentication policies, follow a safe process: backup, modify in a sandbox, test with a test account, and revert if necessary. Start by copying critical PAM files so you can restore them. Next, edit the pam_pwquality line to set the required parameters. After saving, immediately test by adding or changing a test user's password to confirm that weak passwords are rejected and strong ones are accepted. Physical security is often overlooked but critical: if an attacker gains physical access to a server, many software-based protections can be circumvented. Physical controls include locked server rooms, badge access, surveillance, and limiting console access to authorized personnel.
